title: Lt Col Prithi Pal Singh Bedi v Union of India
legal_question: Whether military court-martial procedures and composition conform to statutory and constitutional safeguards, including the role of Army Rule 180.
material_facts: Officers challenged convening and composition of General Courts-Martial, with claims about procedural rights before trial.
holding: Rule 180 protects meaningful participation when an existing Court of Inquiry is likely to affect a person’s character or military reputation; it does not require that a CoI be set up in every disciplinary matter.
commanders_summary: A CoI is not automatically mandatory before every court-martial. Where one is convened and reputation is implicated, the affected person’s Rule 180 rights must be respected. Check statutory composition and procedural safeguards independently.
scope_and_caveats: The decision dates from 1982. Provisions and cases must be checked against later amendments and judicial treatment; a current procedure cannot be inferred from its historical description alone.
what_went_wrong: Mistaking safeguards attached to a CoI for a universal duty to convene a CoI can misdirect the procedure. Conversely, treating a CoI as informal does not remove Rule 180 protections.
source_note: Inherited from v0.1; no independent legal clearance.
review_notes: Inherited unchanged from v0.2. This release does not revalidate its legal analysis.
v04_note: No judgment PDF stored offline; no human legal clearance.
v05_caveat: Judgment dates from 1982. The discussion of then-existing Army Rule 25 and appellate arrangements is historical; Rule 25 was subsequently omitted and the AFT system came later. Verify present Rules and later case law before use.
v05_verified_proposition: Army Rule 180 does not mandate a prior Court of Inquiry before every court-martial. If a Court of Inquiry is convened and a person’s character or military reputation is likely to be affected, the rule requires that person to be afforded meaningful participation.

title: Union of India v Ex Sep Virendra Kumar
legal_question: Can an earlier Rule 180 defect lead the AFT to set aside a completed court-martial and order a de novo CoI?
material_facts: The AFT set aside a dismissal and directed fresh proceedings starting at the Court of Inquiry because the respondent had not participated when witness evidence was recorded.
holding: Rule 180 compliance is obligatory; however, the Court rejected a post-trial de novo CoI remand in the facts because the ground was not raised at charge, Summary of Evidence or trial stages, and AFT retrial powers under Section 16 are limited.
commanders_summary: At an inquiry, give Rule 180 opportunities where triggered. At charge and evidence stages, respond promptly to procedural objections. For challenges after final court-martial, check the precise remedy and prejudice, not a blanket invalidity rule.
scope_and_caveats: This is a fact-specific ruling. It must not be read as permission to ignore mandatory protections or a holding that all CoI violations are harmless.
what_went_wrong: The AFT remedy was framed more broadly than Section 16 allowed; earlier-stage defects were not raised when rectification was feasible.
source_note: Inherited from v0.1; no independent legal clearance.
review_notes: Inherited unchanged from v0.2. This release does not revalidate its legal analysis.
v04_note: No judgment PDF stored offline; no human legal clearance.
v04_verified_holding_note: Army Rule 180 compliance is obligatory, including rectification when a complaint is raised at charge or Summary of Evidence stage. On the facts, the Court rejected the AFT direction for a de novo CoI following a completed court-martial. The Section 16 AFT Act power to order court-martial retrial is confined to its statutory circumstances.
v04_verified_caveat: Not a blanket harmless-error rule; not authority to bypass Rule 180. Subsequent treatment not comprehensively checked. The official PDF contains an apparent heading slip referring to Army Act Section 16 immediately before quoting AFT Act Section 16; cite the statutory text, not that heading.

title: Union of India v Lt Col Kuldeep Yadav
provisions: Policy on censure applicable at incident date
legal_question: When may a tribunal interfere with the nature and severity of administrative censure?
material_facts: An officer challenged the award of Severe Displeasure (Recordable) following admitted lapses; the AFT regarded a less severe form of censure as appropriate.
holding: The Supreme Court restored the competent authority’s decision. Review for disproportionality is circumscribed and reserved for exceptional outcomes that shock the conscience or are patently unreasonable.
commanders_summary: Before awarding censure, record the misconduct, notice, response, applicable policy, and competent authority. In review, distinguish a legally unreasonable outcome from disagreement over the appropriate severity.
scope_and_caveats: The governing censure instructions and the facts of the admission were material. It is not a blanket bar to judicial scrutiny of administrative punishment.
what_went_wrong: Substituting a different sanction merely because it appears preferable is not the same as identifying a reviewable legal error.
source_note: Inherited from v0.1; no independent legal clearance.
review_notes: Inherited unchanged from v0.2. This release does not revalidate its legal analysis.
v04_note: No judgment PDF stored offline; no human legal clearance.
v04_verified_holding_note: Interference with proportionality is possible but exceptional; the Tribunal should not routinely substitute its assessment of punishment. The Court upheld the censure under the then applicable policy and specific facts, rejecting the AFT basis for reducing it.
v04_verified_caveat: The opinion applies a 23 April 2007 censure policy, also referencing a 2017 policy. It is not proof that those instructions govern every current censure. A competent officer should verify contemporary policy and authority before acting.

title: State of Sikkim v Jasbir Singh
legal_question: Does military status necessarily displace the jurisdiction of a Sessions Court for an offence by a soldier?
material_facts: A soldier faced homicide allegations after a shooting in barracks. A criminal court had been directed to transfer the matter for court-martial.
holding: The Supreme Court held the ordinary criminal court was competent in the circumstances, reversed the High Court and directed transfer from military to civil custody for trial.
commanders_summary: Immediately identify offence, victim status, location, custody, statute, and competent authority. Do not assume every offence committed by military personnel must be tried by court-martial.
scope_and_caveats: The decision applies the legal framework in force for the underlying events and litigation; map CrPC/IPC references carefully to post-July 2024 legislation as relevant.
what_went_wrong: The jurisdiction decision was built on the assumption that the military alone must try the offence, without applying concurrent jurisdiction rules to the facts.
source_note: Inherited from v0.1; no independent legal clearance.
review_notes: Inherited unchanged from v0.2. This release does not revalidate its legal analysis.
v04_note: No judgment PDF stored offline; no human legal clearance.
v06_source_evidence: Original Supreme Court judgment indexed on official api.sci.gov.in; paras 41-47, 51-52 checked by reading court text.
v06_review_note: Civil court and military court can have concurrent jurisdiction; facts evidenced Army choice of criminal forum. Current BNSS adaptation and competent authorities require separate review.
v06_verified_holding: Sections 69 and 70 govern overlap; an offence within concurrent jurisdiction does not deprive the criminal court of initial jurisdiction. On the established actions of Army authorities in this case, the Sessions Court was competent. Appeal allowed, accused transferred to civil custody for trial.
v06_scope_caveat: Decision depends on specific conduct showing submission to civilian jurisdiction; not a blanket rule removing notice duties or all military court jurisdiction. Pre-2024 CrPC context.

scope_and_caveats: Not every medical standard was struck down; the Court addressed timing, implementation and disparate impact. Later proceedings may affect particular cohorts and relief.
what_went_wrong: Delayed implementation and historical evaluation practices affected the equality of the selection exercise.

title: Randhir Singh v Union of India
legal_question: When is a Summary Court-Martial legally justified where immediate action is not demonstrated?
material_facts: The incident occurred in August 2007, whereas SCM took place in May 2008, raising doubts about the need for immediate summary trial.
holding: The Court held the SCM contrary to law under the Section 120 framework and provided case-specific pension-related relief under Article 142 in view of lapse of time and impracticability of fresh proceedings.
commanders_summary: Do not default to SCM for convenience. Record legal grounds, time sensitivity, rank/jurisdiction and referrals required by Section 120. Distinguish general SCM rules from exceptional Article 142 relief.
scope_and_caveats: The 2016 Vishav Priya Singh requirement to record SCM reasons was clarified to operate from 5 July 2016; however, statutory constraints still require examination for earlier incidents.
what_went_wrong: A lengthy delay between incident and SCM undermined the claimed need for immediate action.
source_note: Inherited from v0.1; no independent legal clearance.
review_notes: Inherited unchanged from v0.2. This release does not revalidate its legal analysis.
v04_note: No judgment PDF stored offline; no human legal clearance.
v04_verified_holding_note: The Court explained that recording reasons for convening an SCM under the clarified Vishav Priya Singh ruling applies from 5 July 2016; the requirement is prospective. Independently, Section 120(2) restricts SCM resort when there is no grave reason for immediate action. On the case facts, the long interval undermined SCM resort.
v04_verified_caveat: Do not apply the 2016 recording-reasons rule retroactively to every earlier proceeding. The Supreme Court awarded case-specific pension relief under Article 142, not a generic sentencing entitlement.

title: Union of India v Sgt Girish Kumar (main judgment)
legal_question: Whether arrears of broad-banded disability pension in the appealed cases could be restricted to three years before the AFT filing.
material_facts: The batch included former personnel already granted disability pension, who sought reassessment/broad-banding and associated arrears.
holding: The Supreme Court granted the specific appealed claimants arrears from the applicable dates and interest, rejecting the blanket three-year restriction in those cases.
commanders_summary: Identify whether the claimant is already entitled to disability pension and seeks recomputation, or is asserting initial entitlement. Do not convert a case-specific arrears award into a universal entitlement rule.
scope_and_caveats: Read together with the Supreme Court clarification dated 12 October 2026, which expressly prevents mechanical extension to every pension claim.
what_went_wrong: Applying the arrears holding to a claim involving disputed initial disability-pension entitlement would overlook the factual basis of the batch.

title: Union of India v Parashotam Dass
case_number: Civil Appeal No. 447 of 2023 with connected matters
legal_question: How do the High Courts’ Article 226 powers interact with the AFT statutory appeal structure?
material_facts: The dispute examined access to constitutional judicial review of AFT decisions, considering earlier decisions about tribunal jurisdiction and appellate remedies.
holding: The Court distinguished Article 226 judicial review from the Article 227(4) restriction on superintendence and examined the statutory AFT appellate scheme.
commanders_summary: Do not say that AFT decisions are either entirely immune from High Court review or ordinarily appealable in the High Court as of right. Assess maintainability, remedy and grounds.

v04_verified_holding_note: Article 226 judicial review of AFT decisions is not per se barred. title: S N Mukherjee v Union of India
legal_question: Do authorities acting in military adjudicatory or confirmation functions have to provide reasons, and what exceptions matter?
material_facts: A former Army officer challenged court-martial proceedings and confirmation decisions; the Court analysed the general administrative-law duty to give reasons and statutory exceptions.
holding: The Constitution Bench considered reasons in quasi-judicial decisions and construed the THEN operative Army Act/Rules as not requiring reasons for court-martial findings, confirmation or section 164(2) rejection. Later Army Rule 62(1) requires brief reasons for findings on each charge.
commanders_summary: Before advising that a military order must or need not carry reasons, check the precise authority, function, present statute and later precedent.
scope_and_caveats: Historical 1990 statement about court-martial findings must NOT be applied without checking the post-1993 Army Rule 62(1) amendment. Whether confirmation or section 164(2) rejection needs reasons today is a distinct legal question requiring updated case-law review.
what_went_wrong: Applying a general natural-justice maxim without checking a specific statutory exclusion, or using historical exceptions for new decisions.
source_note: Government training institute hosts judgment transcription; check official SCR pagination before approval.

title: Major General Inder Jit Kumar v Union of India
legal_question: What is the nature of a Court of Inquiry and what records or participation rights does the affected officer receive?
material_facts: An Army officer challenged preliminary inquiry and later court-martial steps after proceedings involving alleged impropriety.
holding: A general (not case-specific) COAS warrant can empower a competent officer to convene GCM under Army Act section 109. A CoI is a preliminary fact-finding body; the accused does not automatically have a right to the report as claimed in this case. The Court rejected the case-specific natural justice challenges.
commanders_summary: Separate the fact-finding purpose, Rule 180 opportunities and later disciplinary proof; examine disclosure duties under the relevant rule.
scope_and_caveats: General warrant and attachment findings depend on the lawful instrument and facts. No blanket waiver of Rule 180 protections; current instructions and later judgments must be considered. Secondary transcription only.
what_went_wrong: Assuming CoI findings automatically become admissible trial evidence or all inquiry reports are unconditionally disclosable.

title: Union of India and Others v IC-14827 Major A Hussain
legal_question: What is the High Court review standard for a properly convened court-martial and is a CoI necessarily part of pretrial process?
material_facts: Judicial challenge to court-martial proceedings involving loss of a classified operational brief.
holding: The Supreme Court reversed the High Court after examining the actual opportunities to defend; ordinary defects in investigation do not automatically invalidate a competent court-martial unless a mandatory safeguard or prejudice is involved. Rule 149 does not excuse substantive injustice.
commanders_summary: Check jurisdiction, convening, composition and fairness; do not treat a CoI as a compulsory universal pre-trial stage.
scope_and_caveats: Fact-specific and pre-AFT. It does NOT permit ignoring mandatory safeguards, Rule 180, disclosure duties or denial of genuine defence opportunity. Court-report facsimile located through non-court host; official archive not authenticated.
what_went_wrong: Using the supervisory role of a civil appellate court as a substitute for statutory military trial review.

title: Union of India and Others v Sanjay Jethi and Another
legal_question: How do meaningful Rule 180 participation and an impartial CoI affect a fact-finding inquiry?
material_facts: An affected officer challenged a Court of Inquiry alleging bias and denial of fair procedural participation.
holding: Meaningful Rule 180 participation and impartial inquiry membership were central. The two technical members had prepared evaluative material, creating a legally relevant bias concern; Court sustained the AFT direction for independent additional inquiry. The members of the CoI were NOT automatically cross-examinable as witnesses.

Para 50 rejects a claimed entitlement to cross-examine the presiding officer/technical members simply by status. Cross-check 2020 Virendra Kumar on different circumstances and remedy.
what_went_wrong: Nominal attendance or paper opportunity does not necessarily satisfy meaningful Rule 180 participation.

title: Union of India and Another v Charanjit S Gill and Others
legal_question: What statutory standards apply to a Judge Advocate associated with a General Court-Martial?
material_facts: An accused officer challenged constitution and legal arrangements of court-martial proceedings including the Judge Advocate appointment.
holding: The Judge Advocate at GCM is an integral legal officer whose qualification attracts Rule 40(2) through Rule 102. title: Union of India and Others v Himmat Singh Chahar

title: Union of India and Others v Shivendra Bikaram Singh
material_facts: A Naval lieutenant challenged a court-martial after the trial Judge Advocate summarily rejected his objections to the impartiality of members, instead of following Section 102.
holding: The Court affirmed that non-compliance with the mandatory member-objection procedure vitiated proceedings. It did not approve the High Court's separate merits assessment of evidentiary sufficiency; the competent authority could consider restarting the process lawfully.
